subtopics.title: Constitution and Role of the Commission
subtopics.summary: The 16th Finance Commission was set up in 2023 under Article 280 to recommend how tax revenue is distributed between the Centre and the States. It has one Chairperson, Dr. Arvind Panagariya, and four other members, appointed by the President for a generally five-year tenure. Its report and an Action Taken Memorandum are laid before Parliament under Article 281, and the Government has accepted its key recommendations for 2026-31.

subtopics.title: Vertical and Horizontal Devolution
subtopics.summary: Vertical devolution fixes the share of the Centre's divisible tax pool transferred to the States, which the 16th Commission kept at 41 per cent. Horizontal devolution decides how that 41 per cent is divided among States, and the revised criteria add GDP contribution while reducing the weight of income distance and geographical area. The divisible pool excludes cesses, surcharges and the cost of collection.

subtopics.title: Grants-in-Aid, Cess and Surcharge
subtopics.summary: Statutory grants under Article 275 go only to States in need of financial assistance and are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India every year. Discretionary grants under Article 282 can be made for any public purpose, and the Centre has no obligation to give them. Cesses and surcharges are levied by the Centre and are not shared with States, while SASCI provides long-term interest-free loans for capital projects.

subtopics.title: Fiscal Discipline and Local Bodies
subtopics.summary: The Commission recommends that the Centre's fiscal deficit fall to 3.5 per cent of GDP and the States' limit be set at 3 per cent of GSDP by 2030-31. It also recommends ending off-budget borrowings by States and performance-linked grants for local bodies. For urban areas it proposes an urbanisation premium and a constitutional change regarding State Finance Commission recommendations.

subtopics.title: Impact, Concerns and Past Commissions
subtopics.summary: The retained 41 per cent share is said to give States revenue predictability, and the revised formula is said to safeguard fiscally weaker States. Critics point to the 41 per cent share falling short of the 50 per cent demanded, the reduced weight for demographic performance, and the discontinuation of revenue-deficit grants. Finance Commissions have been appointed since 1951, and the early chairpersons include K.C. Neogy.

quizzes.passage:
The 16th Finance Commission was set up in 2023. It is a constitutional body, which means that its role is laid down in the Constitution itself. Its basic task is to recommend how tax revenues are distributed between the Central Government and the State Governments. Because the sharing of tax revenue lies at the heart of India's federal arrangement, the Commission's work has a direct bearing on the finances of every State.

The Commission works as one body made up of a Chairperson and other members. Each member holds office for a specified tenure. The Commission is constituted at intervals, so it is not a permanent body that works without a break. The 16th Commission is part of a series of such bodies that have been set up since 1951.

The Government has accepted the key recommendations of the Commission for the 2026-31 period. This means that the report now shapes the transfer of resources between the Union and the States during those years. Apart from the division of taxes, the Commission also makes recommendations on grants, so its role covers more than tax sharing alone. The report is a formal document that sets out the Commission's recommendations for the period it covers, and the Commission's work is tied to that period from start to finish.

quizzes.passage:
The 16th Finance Commission was set up in 2023 to recommend how tax revenue is distributed between the Centre and the States. It is a constitutional body, so its role has a formal place in India's federal structure. The Commission consists of a Chairperson and other members, and each member serves for a specified tenure rather than on an open-ended basis.

The President of India constitutes each Finance Commission at intervals, and the recommendations of the 16th Commission cover the period from 2026 to 2031. The Government has accepted the key recommendations for that period.

The report of the Commission is a formal document. It reaches Parliament together with an Action Taken Memorandum, which records the steps the Government has taken on the recommendations. The 16th Commission is part of a long series of Finance Commissions, the first of which was appointed in 1951.

The Commission's recommendations cover a fixed period. Its members are appointed by the President of India, and the Commission works as a single body under its Chairperson. Its scope includes both the sharing of tax revenue between the Centre and the States and the grants that the Constitution allows the Union to make to the States.

quizzes.passage:
The Constitution provides for grants-in-aid from central resources to the States, so the Union can support State finances beyond the sharing of tax revenue. Grants of this kind come in two broad types, and the two types differ in how they are made and in the purposes they serve. Grants are an important part of the financial relationship between the Union and the States.

Some grants are given to States on the basis of the Finance Commission's recommendations, and they are meant for States that need financial help. Others are made by the Centre for purposes it chooses, and these may be given for any public purpose.

Apart from grants, the Centre also collects levies such as the cess and the surcharge. A cess is a levy imposed for a specific purpose, and a surcharge is an extra amount added to the base tax of some taxpayers. The Centre also runs a scheme that provides long-term loans to States.

The booklet treats grants and levies as separate parts of the same financial relationship between the Union and the States. Each part has its own rules, and each affects the amount of money that States finally have at their disposal. Levies such as the cess and surcharge are part of the Centre's own revenue.

quizzes.passage:
Grants-in-aid are one way in which the Union supports the finances of State Governments. The Constitution allows Parliament to make grants to States that need financial assistance, and such grants are not extended to every State. Another category of grants is made by the Centre for any public purpose, and the Centre decides whether to make such grants at all.

Levies are a separate matter. The Centre can impose a cess for a specific purpose, and the money raised must be used for that purpose. A surcharge is an additional tax on top of the base tax, aimed at people with high incomes.

The Centre also runs a scheme that gives States long-term loans for capital projects. The loans support lasting assets that the States create, and they are given over a long repayment period.

The booklet also notes that a cess must be spent on the purpose for which it is levied, and that a surcharge is charged on top of the base tax of those with high incomes. The loans are part of the Centre's support for State governments, and they are meant for the creation of capital projects that last over time. The Centre decides for itself whether to make discretionary grants, and the booklet describes this as lying within its discretion.

quizzes.passage:
Finance Commissions have been a regular feature of India's fiscal federalism since 1951, and each one makes recommendations on how tax revenue is shared between the Centre and the States. The sharing takes place through a divisible pool, and the share given to States from that pool is among the most debated figures in public finance.

The debate has several strands. Some have argued that the share is too low for States' needs, and that States have sought a higher share. Others focus on the formula that splits the States' share among the States, since the weights given to different criteria change the amount each State receives.

The concerns about the formula relate to income, demography and economic performance, and to the effect of those factors on particular regions. Some States point to the features that make them distinct, while others want the formula to reward performance more directly.

The discussion also draws on the earlier Commissions, which were appointed in different years and chaired by different persons, so the record of Finance Commissions forms a long series. In each case the report is a formal recommendation to the Government and is placed before Parliament. This makes each report a formal part of the record of Finance Commissions.

quizzes.passage:
Finance Commissions have been appointed periodically for several decades, and each one makes recommendations on how the Centre's tax revenue should be shared with the States. The sharing is done through a divisible pool, and the share allotted to States from that pool is one of the most debated figures in Indian public finance.

In the 16th Commission's report, the share of the divisible pool given to States has been kept at the existing level, and the Commission has said this will give States greater predictability in their revenue. Some observers have said the level is too low, and that States had sought a larger share from the pool.

The Commission has also revised the formula that decides how the States' share is split among States. The revised criteria are said to protect fiscally weaker States. The report has also drawn concern about the weight given to certain criteria, including the demographic factor, and about the discontinuation of certain grants.

The report of the 16th Commission covers the period from 2026 to 2031, and the Government has accepted its key recommendations for that period. The record of Finance Commissions runs across several decades, from the first Commission onwards, and this report is one of the most recent entries in that record.
